tldr: By coupling two vine robots in parallel and controlling the feed of an externally mounted working channel, this robot achieves both sharp active steering of nearly 90 degrees and tool delivery without blocking the inside of the tubes.
hero_caption: Overall configuration and operating principle of the proposed multi-vine system. The tips of two vine robots are connected via soft fabric caps, holding an external working channel between them. Locking the channel and pressurizing only one side induces buckling to execute sharp turns.
overview:
Soft eversion robots, or "vine robots," grow forward by inverting from the inside of their tube. Because they advance without sliding against surrounding walls, they hold great promise for medical applications such as colonoscopy. However, passive deformation alone is insufficient to navigate sharp bends like the sigmoid colon, requiring active steering. Moreover, routing a working channel inside the robot body to deliver therapeutic tools and sensors creates a dilemma: it strictly constrains tool size, adds internal friction, and limits environmental access strictly to the robot tip.

To solve this, the authors developed a "multi-vine" architecture where two vine robots are arranged in parallel, bridging an external working channel between them via flexible fabric caps. For straight-line growth, both vines are pressurized simultaneously while feeding the channel freely. For turning, the central working channel is locked while pressurizing only the vine on the side opposite the desired turn direction. This induces intentional buckling in the structure, generating a sharp directional turn of nearly 90 degrees.

In experiments using a silicone colon phantom mimicking anatomical dimensions, the system—using two ultra-thin 10 mm diameter vines—successfully delivered an external 6 mm outer-diameter working channel around a high-friction, sharp 90-degree curve to its destination. This opens new possibilities for minimally invasive tool delivery deep within the body.
contributions: Proposed a novel multi-vine architecture coupling two vine robots with an external working channel via soft mounting caps at the tip.
Achieved sharp active steering of nearly 90 degrees without additional actuators by locking the working channel feed and applying asymmetric pneumatic pressure to the vines.
Adopted an external channel approach that does not crowd the robot interior, enabling a thin 10 mm diameter vine configuration to pull a thick 6 mm outer-diameter silicone tube.
Experimentally demonstrated successful navigation through a 90-degree bend inside a high-friction silicone colon phantom.

sections.heading: Why Vine Robots Need Parallel Pairs and External Channels
sections.summary: Vine robots excel at navigating tight anatomical pathways with minimal friction, but active steering through sharp bends and securing a tool channel remained major challenges. This work solves both hurdles at once by bundling two vines and an external channel using soft tip caps.
sections.details:
A vine robot (soft eversion robot) consists of a thin-walled tube folded inward that everts and grows forward from its tip when pressurized. Because it does not rub against surrounding tissues during deployment, it is exceptionally well-suited for navigating delicate, tortuous pathways such as the human colon.

However, real clinical deployment faces two major barriers:
- First is navigating sharp curves. Traditional vine robots rely on passive contact forces with the wall to turn. In sharp turns like the sigmoid colon, growth often halts depending on contact angles and unconstrained lengths, making active steering indispensable. Prior attempts using distributed artificial muscles or dedicated tip steering mechanisms added substantial system complexity.
- Second is payload and tool delivery. Performing diagnosis or therapy requires delivering sensors and microsurgical tools to the target site via a working channel. Previous approaches typically routed the channel inside the eversion tube, which severely constrained tool size, increased internal friction that hindered growth, and limited environmental access solely to the robot tip.

Conducted under the European medical project "EndoTheranostics," this study takes a different approach. Two independent vine robots are placed side by side, and flexible caps fitted over their tips couple them to an external working channel. Without obstructing the interior at all, differential pressure control combined with locking the channel enables sharp steering.

captions.F1: Overall appearance and steering principle of the multi-vine system. Pressurizing only the right vine while the working channel is locked causes the entire assembly to turn sharply to the left. Conversely, pressurizing the left vine turns it to the right.

sections.heading: Buckling-Driven Steering and Robot Fabrication
sections.summary: By braking the feed of the working channel and pressurizing only one vine, intentional structural buckling creates sharp turns of roughly 90 degrees. The robot bodies are fabricated by ultrasonically welding ultrathin polyethylene sheets.
sections.details:
### Operating Principle: Asymmetric Pressurization and Channel Locking for Steering
The control principle of this system is remarkably intuitive and elegant:
- Straight Growth: Equal pneumatic pressure is supplied to both the left and right vines while the central working channel is fed freely.
- Left Turn: With the advancement of the working channel locked by a stopper, only the right vine is pressurized. The right vine attempts to extend, but because the center is restrained, intentional buckling occurs across the structure, steering the robot tip sharply to the left.
- Right Turn: Switching pressure to the left vine steers the robot symmetrically to the right.
- Speed Control: Adjusting the feed rate of the working channel regulates the overall deployment speed of the system and prevents the fabric caps from slipping off the tip.

### Robot Fabrication Details
The physical prototype was built to high-precision specifications with medical applications in mind:
- Vine Bodies: Made from 0.06 mm thick low-density polyethylene (LDPE) sheets. Using a Vetron 5064 ultrasonic welding machine, flat tubes of 1.5 m length with lay-flat widths of 16 mm and 34 mm were produced. Upon pressurization and deployment, their outer diameters measure approximately 10 mm and 20 mm, respectively.
- Working Channel: A silicone tube with an outer diameter of 6 mm was used, providing ample size for endoluminal navigation.
- Soft Tip Caps: Cylindrical sleeves sewn from fabric. Designed with an inner diameter roughly 1 mm larger than the vine outer diameter, they slide smoothly over the everting tip while maintaining their position.
- Actuation Base: A chamber made by fused filament 3D printing houses motor-controlled spools that feed the folded vine material. Pneumatic pressure is regulated using high-precision electropneumatic regulators (SMC ITV2050).

sections.heading: Open-Space Pipe Entry and Colon Phantom Trials
sections.summary: After verifying that vine deployment pressures possess a safe margin below burst limits, the robot demonstrated entering pipe openings in open space and navigating a 90-degree bend inside a high-friction silicone colon phantom.
sections.details:
### Characterization of Deployment Pressures
First, minimum deployment pressures and burst limits were measured for single vines of 10 mm and 20 mm diameters. The narrower 10 mm vine required around 35 kPa due to higher internal inversion friction, higher than the 20 mm vine (around 13 kPa). However, the 10 mm vine had a burst pressure of approximately 105 kPa (around 60 kPa for the 20 mm vine), ensuring an adequate safety margin above operating pressures. Additionally, attaching the fabric soft cap had negligible effect on the minimum deployment pressure.

### Steering Demonstration in Open Space
In an open-space test using 20 mm diameter vines, the robot smoothly transitioned from straight-line growth to controlled turns to either side. Furthermore, it successfully demonstrated active steering toward the entrance of a curved pipe, entering and deploying inside the pipe accurately.

### Navigation in a Silicone Colon Phantom
To mimic clinical conditions, trials were conducted in a silicone colon phantom modeled after human anatomical dimensions. Compared to living colonic mucosa, silicone is non-slippery and presents an unforgiving, high-friction environment. Nevertheless, the multi-vine robot using two 10 mm diameter vines successfully negotiated a tight 90-degree curve while pulling the 6 mm outer-diameter working channel. This proved sufficient propulsive capability to clear steep bends while maintaining the tip camera's field of view.

(b) Steering and entering the opening of a curved pipe in an open environment. (c) Experimental trial traversing a 90-degree bend inside a silicone colon phantom while carrying the working channel.

sections.heading: Reducing Tissue Stress and Enabling Longitudinal Access
sections.summary: This approach replaces painful passive passage that pushes against intestinal walls with active, safe navigation. The external channel relieves tool size constraints, opening pathways toward procedures that deploy instruments anywhere along the robot body.
sections.details:
The multi-vine architecture presented here neatly resolves the long-standing trade-off between steering and tool delivery in vine robots.

Even a vine robot significantly narrower than the colon diameter (e.g., around 1 cm) can passively deform to advance. However, sharp curves inevitably rely on high reaction forces exerted against the bowel wall, carrying risks of patient discomfort or tissue injury. In contrast, an active steering system that bends itself via differential actuation and structural buckling—like this system—drastically lowers excessive wall contact forces, safely navigating tortuous anatomy.

An even more crucial advantage is having the working channel located on the outside. Because instruments do not need to squeeze through a cramped internal tube cavity, larger and more diverse microsurgical tools can be delivered. Looking ahead, the authors highlight future directions including detailed quantitative characterization of turning dynamics, full motorization of the channel feed, and developing mechanisms that allow tools to access the external environment from any point along the robot body, rather than just the tip.

takeaways: A remarkably simple yet effective active steering mechanism: sandwiching an external channel between two vines, locking the channel, and pressurizing one side to induce sharp buckling turns.
Mounting the channel externally bypasses internal friction that impedes growth, allowing delivery of thicker therapeutic instruments.
Demonstrated real-world capability by clearing a 90-degree turn in a silicone colon phantom with higher friction than biological tissue, all while carrying a realistically sized working channel.
Suggests expandable future medical workflows unique to external channels, such as accessing anatomy along the full length of the robot body rather than just the tip.
limitations: The working channel feed is currently controlled manually, and full automated coordination with the vine deployment motors has not yet been implemented.
Kinematic and dynamic quantitative characterization—such as precise steering angles, generated forces, and turning radii—remains to be fully conducted.

Bundling two vines and an external channel in parallel creates an asymmetric cross-section compared to a single vine, requiring further investigation into torsional stiffness and snagging risks in narrow anatomical passages.
